paras: The whitecapping of George and Amelia Guenther was a night attack on 9 October 1903 in which about a dozen masked men fired into the farmhouse of George Guenther, a white farmer near Sandusky, Ohio, and his Black wife, whom he had recently married. One bullet wounded both, and in November a grand jury indicted five Perkins Township men. Papers nationwide presented the attack as neighbors punishing an interracial marriage, and Black weeklies condemned the attackers.

Guenther, described as wealthy, was about 60; his wife, born Amelia Harris, was about 30 and, according to the Cleveland Gazette, his former cook and the daughter of "an old soldier" whose land adjoined his. A special dispatch to the St. Paul Globe reported that on a Monday night in early October a crowd of Perkins citizens gave the couple ten days to leave the country and threatened "mob law." A later Sandusky dispatch said would-be whitecappers had also come on the wedding night and were driven off by Guenther and his son with shotguns.

At about 10 o'clock on the night of 9 October, a dozen masked men with shotguns and revolvers surrounded the house, five miles from Sandusky, and riddled it with bullets. One bullet struck Amelia Guenther in the arm and then glanced to strike her husband on the forehead. The couple fled to the barn and stayed there in their nightclothes until 5:30 the next morning, while the attackers lingered until nearly daylight. The furniture was riddled and 36 panes of glass broken, in what the wire called the third attack since the marriage.

The next morning the Guenthers sought warrants in Sandusky but could give no names. On 22 October an Ohio news column reported that they had not returned home and that "more drastic measures" might follow if they did. Two days later the Cleveland Gazette reported that Guenther and his son Jack were armed and meant to stay.

Judge Reed of Sandusky asked the grand jury to indict the mob's leaders. On 9 November it indicted five Perkins Township men, withholding their names until arrests, and took more time to investigate alleged perjury by witnesses. No report of arrests or a trial was found.

The wire story ran on 10 October in papers from Alexandria to Spokane, and the New York Sun headed it "HOUSE RIDDLED WITH BULLETS." White headlines centered the marriage, such as "White Man Punished For Marrying a Negress" in the Stark County Democrat and "PEOPLE WON'T STAND FOR MISCEGENATION" in the St. Paul Globe. The wire text said "this mixture of races" had stirred the neighbors, and the Savannah Morning News mocked "the chromatic sensibilities of Ohioans."

Black weeklies took up the story a week later. The Baltimore Afro-American reprinted the wire account, while the Chicago Broad Ax called the attackers "bloodthirsty white savages" and regretted that Guenther had not killed them. The St. Paul Appeal remarked that there would have been no trouble had Guenther "lived in adultery with the woman." The Cleveland Gazette called the attackers "masked brutes (white)" and greeted the family's armed stand with "Good!"

Two short early dispatches said the couple were dragged into the woods and "maltreated" or that Guenther was beaten and his wife might die. The fuller wire account and later Sandusky reports describe a shooting from outside, with the couple "slightly injured." The count of attacks also varied, from three in the wire to two in the indictment reports.

reader.title: Whitecapping of George and Amelia Guenther
bases: A masked night band, called 'white caps' and 'whitecappers' in the reports, shot up the couple's home after a crowd had ordered them to leave the country within ten days (A1, A2, A8, A21).

Independent wire versions, an Ohio state-news column and the Black press agree on a night shooting attack on the Guenther home, and later Sandusky reports record five indictments (A2, A8, A15, A16, A21).

accounts.label: Main wire report (Sandusky, Oct. 10)
accounts.gist: A dozen masked men shot up the house; one bullet slightly wounded both; the couple hid in the barn until morning; third attack since the marriage.

accounts.label: Alternative wire version
accounts.gist: The couple were taken from the house, dragged into the woods and maltreated or beaten; the woman seriously hurt and possibly dying.

accounts.label: Springfield special to the St. Paul Globe
accounts.gist: Before the shooting, a crowd of Perkins citizens gave the couple ten days to leave and threatened mob law; Guenther was preparing to sell out.

accounts.label: Guenther's own statement
accounts.gist: He had known his wife nearly all her life, would stick to her, and meant to stay on the farm.

accounts.label: Grand jury report (Sandusky, Nov. 9)
accounts.gist: Five Perkins Township men indicted; witnesses accused of perjury; whitecaps had visited twice, first ordering him to leave, then shooting out the windows.

framing.detail: The wire text, headed 'White Cappers' and 'HOUSE RIDDLED WITH BULLETS', said 'this mixture of races' had stirred the neighbors.
Headlines centered the marriage: 'White Man Punished For Marrying a Negress', 'Neighbors "White-cap" a Man who Marries a Negress', 'PEOPLE WON'T STAND FOR MISCEGENATION'.
The Savannah Morning News used the case to mock Ohioans' 'chromatic sensibilities' without condemning the attack.
The Broad Ax called the attackers 'bloodthirsty white savages' and 'red-handed assassins'; the Appeal derided 'Caucasian civilization and Christianity'.
The Cleveland Gazette rewrote the wire with 'masked brutes (white)' and cheered the family's armed stand with 'Good!'.
The Baltimore Afro-American ran the wire account under 'WHITE FARMER MARRIES'.
